title: Two-day ICMR-SHINE 2026 concludes, igniting scientific curiosity across thousands of young minds
subtitle:
From remote terrains to rural regions, ICMR-SHINE takes biomedical research closer to young minds across 83 locations in 31 States and Union Territories, contributing to a Swasth and Viksit Bharat
Students gain first-hand exposure to Mobile BSL-3 laboratories in Nagpur and Gorakhpur, live scientific demonstrations and hands-on activities nationwide
Young innovators showcase public health solutions through Atal Tinkering Labs in Delhi
ICMR launched SHINE website and announced nationwide school competition on real-world public health challenges, with applications open till 11 September 2026
Schools and teachers welcome research exposure, call for more frequent engagement with students
body_text:
The Department of Health Research - Indian Council of Medical Research (DHR-ICMR) successfully concluded the second edition of ICMR-SHINE (Science & Health Innovation for the Nextgen Explorers) on 11–12 August 2026, bringing the world of biomedical and public health research closer to school students across the country. Taking forward the Prime Minister’s call to “spend a day as a scientist,” the nationwide outreach program opened the doors of ICMR laboratories to students of Classes 9 to 12, giving them an opportunity to see, experience, and interact directly with the science behind public health.
The initiative spanned 31 States and Union Territories across 83 unique locations, stretching far beyond major metropolitan centers into the quiet valleys and remote terrains of Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Andamans and rural regions of Jharkand, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh. For thousands of students who had never experienced research environment, ICMR-SHINE offered a welcoming bridge into the world of biomedical inquiry. Guided by Dr Curio, the friendly official mascot featured across interactive videos, posters, and cut-outs, the atmosphere was designed to make complex science feel inviting, accessible, and fun.
In Nagpur and Gorakhpur, students stepped near state-of-the-art Mobile BSL-3 laboratories on wheels, witnessing firsthand how high-containment research travels directly to field situations. In other centers, young visitors took part in lively poster walks, live scientific demonstrations, and practical exercises on body mass index calculation and lab hygiene, learning how everyday health decisions connect to the broader picture of national public health. In Delhi, the spirit of youth innovation was on full display as students showcased creative solutions developed through Atal Tinkering Labs under NITI Aayog, proving that great scientific ideas have no age limit.
As a part of this initiative, ICMR launched the official SHINE website ( https://shine.icmr.org.in/ ), providing students with access to resources, program updates and opportunities related to health research. ICMR has also announced a nationwide SHINE school competition, inviting students to identify real-world public health challenges, frame research questions and propose potential solutions. The competition will take the idea of “spending a day as a scientist” a step further by encouraging students to look at the health challenges around them through the lens of scientific inquiry and innovation. Applications are open until 11 September 2026 and can be submitted on the SHINE portal.
The initiative received an encouraging response from participating schools across the country. Teachers welcomed the program for giving students valuable exposure to scientific research and laboratory work beyond the classroom, and suggested that it be held more frequently. The school competition also generated enthusiasm, with one participating school announcing that all its students would take part, with submissions counting towards their internal project assessment during school examination.
Through ICMR-SHINE, thousands of students have moved from simply learning about science to seeing it, experiencing it and asking questions about it. By taking research experiences beyond conventional centers and into schools and field locations across the country, the program is creating opportunities for young minds, regardless of where they live, to encounter science firsthand. ICMR is helping young students develop a scientific outlook, encouraging them to explore science, pursue innovation, and play a role in building a Swasth and Viksit Bharat .

ministry.name: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

enrichment.summary: ICMR concluded the second edition of its nationwide outreach programme 'ICMR-SHINE' (Science & Health Innovation for the Nextgen Explorers) on 11-12 August 2026, covering 83 locations across 31 States and UTs and engaging school students of Classes 9-12 with biomedical and public health research. Highlights included exposure to Mobile BSL-3 laboratories in Nagpur and Gorakhpur, science demonstrations, and a showcase of innovations from Atal Tinkering Labs in Delhi. ICMR also launched a dedicated SHINE website and announced a nationwide school competition on real-world public health challenges, with applications open till 11 September 2026.
enrichment.context: ICMR-SHINE reflects a broader push by India's premier biomedical research body to popularize science and build a scientific temper among young students, echoing the Prime Minister's call to 'spend a day as a scientist.' Such outreach initiatives are part of India's efforts to strengthen its science, technology and innovation ecosystem at the grassroots level, complementing programmes like the Atal Tinkering Labs under NITI Aayog's Atal Innovation Mission, which aims to cultivate creativity and problem-solving skills in school children. The involvement of Mobile BSL-3 (Biosafety Level-3) laboratories is notable given India's post-pandemic emphasis on decentralized, field-deployable diagnostic and research infrastructure for high-risk pathogens, a capacity gap exposed during COVID-19. By extending research exposure beyond metropolitan centers into remote areas like Jammu & Kashmir, Arunachal Pradesh, the Andamans and rural Jharkhand, Odisha and Madhya Pradesh, the programme also aligns with the government's broader goal of equitable access to scientific opportunity, feeding into the vision of a 'Swasth aur Viksit Bharat' (Healthy and Developed India) by 2047. ICMR, functioning under the Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, is India's apex body for formulation, coordination and promotion of biomedical research, and such outreach also serves to build a future talent pipeline for public health research.

prelims_questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR):
1. It functions under the Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
2. It is India's apex body for the formulation, coordination and promotion of biomedical research.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims_questions.explanation: As stated in the release, ICMR operates under the Department of Health Research (DHR) within the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and it is India's premier body for biomedical research coordination and promotion.

prelims_questions.question: The 'Atal Tinkering Labs', mentioned in the context of ICMR-SHINE 2026, are implemented under which of the following?
options: Ministry of Education's Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan
Council of Scientific and Industrial Research
prelims_questions.explanation: The release explicitly notes that students showcased solutions developed through Atal Tinkering Labs under NITI Aayog, which runs the Atal Innovation Mission to foster innovation and entrepreneurship among school students.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of school-level scientific outreach programmes like ICMR-SHINE in building India's research and innovation ecosystem. How can such initiatives help bridge the rural-urban divide in access to scientific opportunities?
Examine the role of mobile high-containment laboratories (such as Mobile BSL-3 labs) in strengthening India's public health preparedness and field-level biomedical research capacity.
